passage:
Advisor's note, Wednesday. Nazia writing about Amandeep's two offers.
Amandeep had spread two papers across my table. One offered the bigger number. The other offered less but asked for less in return.
"The big number is loud," Amandeep said, ticking a list. "But it wants two board seats, and if the company is sold, it takes its money back first. The smaller one leaves me in control of the product. And I phoned three founders they backed: the second investor answers calls at night, the first one goes quiet."
It was hard not to say which one I preferred. I asked only what else needed checking. Amandeep decided to have a lawyer read both, and to wait until Friday before answering.
— Nazia

qa.a: Nazia found it hard to stay quiet about a personal preference, and so asked only what else needed checking.

subtype: Approach: comparing term sheets on more than valuation [Thinking]
passage:
Shreya's diary, Sunday.
Two offers on the table and my head is spinning. Offer one is bigger: a higher valuation, the kind of number you'd brag about. Offer two is smaller.
But tonight I made a list instead of just staring at the headline.
Board seats: offer one wants two seats on a board of three. They could outvote us. Offer two wants one seat, and only as an observer for the first year.
Liquidation preference: under offer one, if we sell, they get twice their money back before anyone else. Offer two, just once.
Help: I called three founders each fund had backed. Offer one's founders were polite but vague. Offer two's founders all said the same thing: "They picked up the phone when things went wrong."
Arohi, my co-founder, says the big number is tempting, and she's not wrong. But I'll ask our lawyer to explain both on Tuesday before we choose.

qa.q: How many board seats does offer one want?
qa.a: Two seats on a board of three.

qa.q: How is Shreya feeling while comparing the offers?
qa.a: Shreya feels overwhelmed at first, with a spinning head, but steadier once the list is made.

qa.q: Why is calling founders the funds had backed a good step?
qa.a: It shows how each investor behaves when things go wrong, which a headline number can't show.

qa.q: How does Arohi see the bigger offer?
qa.a: Arohi finds the big number tempting, which Shreya admits is a fair point.

grounding: It shows a founder weighing two offers on board seats, control, liquidation preference and how investors treat founders, not just the higher valuation.
